name: Sous Vide Glazed Carrots
headnote: J. Kenji Lopez-Alt concedes that sous vide is the wrong tool for most vegetables but argues carrots are the exception, because sealing them with butter, sugar and salt concentrates their own juices into something that tastes more like carrot than the raw vegetable did. The temperature is set by chemistry rather than preference: pectin, the glue holding plant cells together, does not break down until 183F, so the bath has to run at least that hot for tender results, which also rules out improvised beer-cooler setups. After the bath the whole contents of the bag go into a hot skillet for a couple of minutes so the liquid reduces to a glossy glaze, with a splash of water to rescue it if it breaks. He notes the same treatment works for small onions, radishes, turnips, parsnips and baby artichokes.
comment_digest: Timing is the sticking point. One cook ran five whole carrots for 70 minutes at 183F and still found them quite firm, guessing another twenty minutes was needed and wondering whether her circulator was underperforming; others report 185F for an hour, or 185F for about 90 minutes with thick carrot coins, as their sweet spot. A faster variation: halve the carrots lengthwise, weight the bag, run 194F for fifteen minutes, then saute, for a deliberately al dente result. Kenji himself answers a floating-bag complaint, explaining that trapped air and water vapour expand at these high temperatures and that the fix is weighting the bag with a water-filled bag or a binder clip on something heavy. Several cooks skip the sugar in favour of maple syrup, honey or brown sugar, or add granular chicken bouillon. One reviewer rejects the method outright in favour of microwave-steaming.
flags: The article portion is short, only a few paragraphs before the recipe, so the headnote material is thinner than on the other pages. A sizeable share of the reviews are unanswered questions (reheating, green beans) or long off-topic anecdotes. Comments truncated at 'Read More'.
